papers.title: Cross-platform multi-laboratory screening identifies HUWE1, USP33 and USP20 as negative-regulators of autophagy or mitophagy with relevance to neurodegeneration
papers.summary: This study used multiple screening platforms across different labs to find genes that normally suppress autophagy and mitophagy, the cellular processes that clear damaged proteins and mitochondria. They identified three enzymes, HUWE1, USP33, and USP20, as key negative regulators, meaning blocking them boosts these cleanup pathways. Because faulty mitophagy and autophagy are linked to neurodegenerative diseases, these enzymes could be promising drug targets.
papers.why: Since HUWE1, USP33, and USP20 act as brakes on mitophagy and autophagy, they are highly relevant candidate targets for understanding and potentially enhancing neuronal quality-control pathways central to this PhD project.

papers.title: Nitric oxide signaling and mitophagy in Parkinson's disease: implications for aerobic exercise-related neuroprotection.
papers.summary: This paper discusses how nitric oxide (NO) signaling influences mitophagy, the process by which cells clear damaged mitochondria, in the context of Parkinson's disease. It explores how dysregulated NO and impaired mitophagy contribute to neuronal damage in this neurodegenerative disorder. The paper also suggests that aerobic exercise may offer neuroprotection by modulating these pathways, potentially through improved mitochondrial quality control.
papers.why: Understanding NO-mediated regulation of mitophagy in neurons provides mechanistic insight relevant to neuronal health and degeneration, directly informing the mitophagy/autophagy focus of the PhD project even though this paper lacks spatial omics or AI components.

papers.title: Fructooligosaccharides Restore Gut Function and Increase Hippocampal Short-Chain Fatty Acids to Alleviate Neuronal Apoptosis Induced by Mitochondrial Autophagy in rats with Chronic Cerebral Hypoperfusion.
papers.summary: This study looked at how fructooligosaccharides (FOS), a type of prebiotic fiber, affect rats with chronic reduced blood flow to the brain. The researchers found that FOS improved gut health and boosted short-chain fatty acids in the hippocampus, which in turn reduced neuronal death linked to excessive mitochondrial autophagy (mitophagy). The findings suggest a gut-brain connection where dietary fiber can protect brain cells from damage caused by poor blood flow through modulating mitochondrial quality control processes.
papers.why: This paper connects to the profile's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons and offers a gut-brain axis mechanism that could inform how systemic/metabolic factors influence mitochondrial quality control relevant to interneuron vulnerability in the hippocampus.

papers.title: Amniotic fluid stem cells alleviate neuronal injury-related changes in spina bifida by inducing autophagy via regulating the FOXO1/STAT3 axis.
papers.summary: This study investigates how amniotic fluid stem cells (AFSCs) may help protect neurons from injury in spina bifida, a birth defect involving incomplete spinal cord closure. The researchers found that AFSCs work by activating autophagy, a cellular cleanup process, through control of the FOXO1/STAT3 signaling pathway. This suggests AFSCs could be a therapeutic approach to reduce neuronal damage associated with this condition.
papers.why: The paper's focus on autophagy regulation via the FOXO1/STAT3 axis in neuronal injury offers mechanistic insight into autophagy pathways that may be relevant background for studying mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation in neurons, even though it centers on a developmental spinal cord context rather than brain interneurons or perineuronal nets.

papers.title: AMPK activation by Aldometanib from Bigujing improves metabolic and cognitive dysfunction in aging mice.
papers.summary: This study investigates Aldometanib, a compound derived from Bigujing, as an activator of AMPK, a key cellular energy-sensing enzyme. In aging mice, this compound was shown to improve both metabolic function and cognitive performance. The findings suggest AMPK activation could be a therapeutic strategy for age-related metabolic and cognitive decline.
papers.why: AMPK is a central regulator of autophagy and mitophagy pathways, making this compound's cognitive benefits in aging mice relevant to understanding neuronal quality-control mechanisms, though the paper lacks direct focus on interneurons, perineuronal nets, or spatial omics methods central to the profile.

papers.title: Puerarin Attenuates Binge Ethanol-Induced Cortical Neurotoxicity in Association with AKT/mTOR Signaling and Autophagy-Related Responses.
papers.summary: This study investigates how puerarin, a natural plant compound, protects brain cortical neurons from damage caused by binge alcohol exposure. The researchers found that puerarin's protective effects are linked to changes in the AKT/mTOR signaling pathway and autophagy-related processes. This suggests puerarin may help reduce alcohol-induced brain cell death by modulating cellular self-degradation mechanisms.
papers.why: Since only an abstract is provided without methodological details, its relevance is limited but touches on autophagy regulation in neurons, a core theme of the profile.

papers.title: SUMOylated Reptin maintains low intracellular ROS levels by activating mitophagy to drive gemcitabine resistance in gallbladder cancer.
papers.summary: This paper studies how a protein called Reptin, when modified by SUMOylation, helps gallbladder cancer cells survive chemotherapy. It shows that this modified Reptin activates mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, which keeps harmful reactive oxygen species (ROS) low inside cancer cells. Because ROS levels stay low, the cancer cells become resistant to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine.
papers.why: Although this is a cancer paper unrelated to neurons or the brain, it offers mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation via SUMOylation and ROS control that could inform how similar pathways operate in neuronal mitophagy studies.

papers.title: The Secretome Derived From Human Umbilical Cord Mesenchymal Stem Cells Improves Skin Photoaging by Enhancing Mitophagy to Inhibit the cGAS-STING Pathway.
papers.summary: This study investigates how a secretome (mix of secreted factors) from human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells can protect skin cells from UV-induced photoaging. The researchers found that this treatment boosts mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, which in turn suppresses the cGAS-STING pathway, an inflammatory signaling cascade activated by mitochondrial DNA damage. The result is reduced signs of skin aging caused by UV exposure, suggesting mitophagy enhancement as a therapeutic strategy against photoaging.
papers.why: Although this paper focuses on skin rather than brain tissue, it provides mechanistic insight into mitophagy regulation and its link to the cGAS-STING inflammatory pathway, which could inform parallel investigations of mitophagy dysfunction in neurons and neuroinflammation.
